title: Strengthening pesticide management in agriculture to reduce risks to health and environment
description:
1.1:  Review and propose improvements in national legislations, regulations, policies, plans and SOP in view of effective management of pesticides and risk reduction;

1.2   Design curricula, conduct ToT and in country trainings on pesticide risk analysis;

1.3:  Develop/adapt training modules and curricula for pesticide management   and risk reduction training for the pesticide regulators and inspectors;

1.4:    Conduct pesticide management and risk reduction training for government staff involved in EIA/IEE, import and handling, registration and approval of pesticides and their compliance monitoring, and policy making;

1.5:  Using FAO Guidelines, develop pesticide registration guidelines for different types of pesticides and pesticide registration software Pesticide Registration and Management Section under Plant Protection Directorate;

2.1: Develop Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) for the RBRP laboratories established for pesticide residue analysis

2.2: Organize abroad training for two laboratory analysts in lab handling, pesticide analysis and residues analysis;

2.3:  Conduct hands on in-country training of laboratory analysts and technicians on pesticide residues analysis using RBPR;

2.4: Provide AChE-Test reagents, chemicals and Spectrophotometers with RBPR programme pack, lab accessories and computers necessary for the hands-on in-country training in RBPR labs;

2.5: Support RBPR labs for field verification of pesticide applications and sample verification of tests from public and private sector laboratories.

3.1: Using FAO Guidelines, develop Code of Practices (CoP) for pesticide manufacturers, importers, agro-vets (retailers) and applicators;

3.2: Develop training modules and curricula incorporating the CoP for training of pesticide entrepreneurs, agro-vets (retailers), and traders;

3.3:  Conduct training of pesticide entrepreneurs, retailers, and traders.

3.4: Develop and demonstrate a pesticide recording system for agrovets to keep information on purchases, sales and uses of pesticides.  

4.1:  Develop/adapt training modules and materials including CoP for farmers for efficient use and handling of pesticide and other chemical inputs;

4.2:  Organize refresher ToT on IPM based GAP, CoP on pesticide handling and management to 60 IPM Farmers’ Facilitators (15 in each of the 4 districts) for safer crop production;

4.3 Conduct 60 trainings (15 in each district) to the established crop producer groups on IPM based GAP, CoP on pesticide handling and management for safer crop production

4.4: Conduct  training to 60 established crop producer groups on internal group based quality assurance system for safer crop production (IPM based) and maintaining traceability of the farm products;

4.5: Provide follow up support to the farmers’ groups to consolidate and strengthen the compliance procedures on IPM GAP, CoP on pesticide handling and group based internal quality assurance system for production of safer products;

4.6: Establish/Strengthen and register Community Resource Centers (1 per  project district) for production of biological and  botanical pest control agents, facilitation of plant clinics in coordination with DADOs and disseminate messages on CoP of  pesticide handing and management  to wider farming community;

5.1:  Document success stories and good practices on pesticide management and disseminate to wider users;

5.2: Develop ICT materials (printed materials, newspaper articles, video/audio jingles etc.) for launching mass media campaign on pesticide problems;

5.3: Launch mass media campaign in collaboration with consumers’ organizations to create awareness on pesticide residues, and their health and environmental implications.

title: Sustainable Urban Environment
description:
• Participatory planning, including revision and rolling process of community plans presented to LAs and other stakeholders on an annual basis in all slums in the 3 towns where we have worked before, and in selected slums in the other 3 towns.
  • Establishment or strengthening of 2 town-wide slum dweller organisations
  • Capacity building training, and assessment of capacity and representativeness of the local organisations through annual review processes and tools for self-assessment
  • Particular focus on needs specific to the communities we are working with, and to marginalised sections within those communities.
  • Building the capacity of LA officials and elected representatives, and establishing systems so that expertise and approaches are passed on effectively to new post-holders
  • city-level forums for co-ordination between stakeholders, giving priority to the needs of slum dwellers, and allocating resources to support their priorities
  • City-level working groups established or strengthened to deal with specific issues
  • Leverage of resources to support community infrastructure priorities from LAs, national programmes and other stakeholders, with the proportion contributed by project resources declining over the course of the project
  • Delivery and management of community infrastructure services (water supply, improved drainage, cluster-latrines, internal roads and paths etc)
  • Exchange visits and other tools which help communities to effectively choose and adapt the types of technologies most appropriate to their situations
  • Promoting the uptake of household-level infrastructure (e.g. household latrines, biogas, home composting, water vending, and incremental housing improvements)
  • Income generation through service delivery with small enterprises in, latrine construction, pit emptying, and waste collection and recycling
  • Peer-learning workshops and building relationships
  • Sharing knowledge and good practices with national and regional municipal associations, networks of NGOs, and slum dweller networks
  • Providing materials (case studies and training modules) for national and regional training institutes
  • Influencing nationwide programmes to adopt elements of the project’s approach for wider scaling up
  • Project regional workshops and visits for synthesising lessons from the 3 countries (Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka)
  • Dissemination of lessons regionally and internationally through conferences and publications

Component 1:Policy Support

Major activities

·      Provide information on international good practice for strategy design, policy and implementation Programs

Component 2: Energy Efficiency in Households

This component has two subcomponents.

A.    To reduce the specific electricity consumption of grid connected households

B.     To reduce the biomass consumption of rural households

Major activities for subcomponent 2A

·       Support awareness raising for households and capacity building for institutions implementing and enforcing the mandatory minimum standards

Major activities for subcomponent 2B

·       Support a study to conceptualize the accelerated dissemination of improved efficient cooking stoves. The study takes socioeconomic, gender and cultural aspects of the target groups into account.

·       Support management, implementation and monitoring of scaling up programmes under AEPC.

Major activities: It is envisaged that relevant private sector institutions found and operate an Energy Efficiency centre. The centre shall operate and provide services on commercial principles while being supported to perform the following activities

·      Training of energy auditors and energy managers

·      Capacity development of chambers of Industry and the financial sector

·      Quality control of energy audits and clearing house for disputes

·      Evaluation and monitoring of impacts resulting from investments in energy efficiency in industry with regard to productivity and profitability.

title: Mediating Local Conflict and Reducing Vulnerability Post Earthquake Recovery (Nepal)
description: The Conflict Mediation in Post Earthquake Recovery supports Nepal's long term recovery following the devastating earthquake on 25 April 2015. The early recovery package of support will focus on three key themes: meeting the educational needs of vulnerable children, with a focus on girls and children with disabilities, as they transition back to school and “building back better” ; rebuilding livelihoods of women and other vulnerable populations; and rebuilding social cohesion, by ensuring there is access to alternative dispute resolution for addressing disaster-related conflict, violence and exploitation of women. Within the early recovery package, Australia provided funds to the Asia Foundation (TAF) in Nepal for a program to address conflicts and vulnerabilities related to earthquake recovery and assistance in Nepal. The program will address, in particular, disputes related to identity, resettlement, land and resource use, and gender-based violence (GBV). The program will support facilitated dialogue, and community mediation in order to create and sustain an enabling environment for effective earthquake recovery efforts. The total value of this investment is $3.0 million over 2 years, starting May 2015.

title: 549NEP5000 (CI) - Empowering people to enjoy their Right to Information for greater accountability of Nepal's power holders
description:
1.2.3. Describe and define the target groups and final beneficiaries, their needs and constraints and how the action will address these needs

Target groups:
The three main target groups are journalists, local "change agents" (teachers, lawyers and civil society activists) and government officials.
The 250 journalists to be selected to participate in the training provided by the project come from the areas mostly affected by press freedom violations. These incidents have been, since 2007, most intense in Nepal's central plains and the eastern hills. Therefore, while journalists in the capital and urban centres have been largely secure, those working in the plains in general and in the eastern hills have been attacked, threatened, or continuously harassed by different interest groups, many of which are also armed. Therefore this project will focus mainly on these areas, where, according to FNJ estimates, there are around 1,500 journalists in the eastern region and around 1,500 to 2,000 journalists in the central plains. These are the areas where working as a journalist is most dangerous, and where the journalists need most support in building their capacity both in investigative journalism and personal safety. Many of these journalists have not had any training in journalism, and do not understand their possibilities and responsibilities in serving the public with accurate, non-partisan information. Therefore through building their capacity, we can improve the access to information for people on district level. The journalists will be selected in cooperation with the local chapters of Federation of Nepali journalists, ensuring equal representation of women, lower castes and other marginalized groups. A special focus will be given to journalists who have already made attempts to practice investigative journalism, but who do not necessarily have the necessary skills yet.
The 250 local mediators (teachers, lawyers and civil society activists, depending on the area) are people who are active in their community and to whom people come to ask for help. These mediators will be trained as local focal points to raise awareness on the RTI Act and its relevance locally as well as for helping local people with their information requests to the government offices. In order to increase the synergies between project components the local mediators will be selected from the same areas as the journalists. That way the journalists and mediators can support each other's work.
The third target group of the project are government officials who are responsible for the implementation of the Right to Information law. Many government offices have information officers, but in many cases their capacity remains low. By organizing local level orientation sessions for the government information officers the project seeks to build their capacity and to orient them to their public service task. In addition, through linking the trained journalists and mediators to these sessions, the project aims at building local level multi-stakeholder networks that on a local level work jointly to increase and improve people's access to public information.

The project mainstreams gender throughout all its activities. In addition, the project will ensure women's equal participation in all training programmes. Individual women will be identified and encouraged to apply, and the trainings will be organized in a manner that suits the time constraints of women.
It is much more challenging for a woman to step up and speak for herself because of the cultural and social norms of gender in Nepal, let alone to demand for information from government officials who often are men. In addition, a woman is likely to be treated differently from a man if she approaches a government office and requests for information. This specific approach will be emphasized in the training of local mediators, so that they will be able to offer locally-relevant solutions - e.g. cooperating with local women's groups, where the information request does not come from an individual woman but a group of women could help ease the social challenges. In addition, the issue of gender equality and women's specific needs will be addressed also in the orientation given to government officials.
The gender equality aspect will also be covered in the handbook for journalists and the handbook for local mediators, both to be published in the course of the project. In addition, the project will ensure all promotional products, such as posters or leaflets, go through a gender analysis, ensuring the material is also suitable for women and doesn't support gender stereotypes.

The overall objective of this action is to improve the transparency of Nepal's government and the accountability of decision-making through a broader implementation of the Right to Information Act. The action also has three specific objectives: 1) Citizens have access to information that is relevant to them and are hence motivated to exercise their democratic rights; 2) Journalists recognize their role as the watchdogs of the power holders and proactively seek and publish correct and timely information and 3) Local level government officials understand their role as public servants and are more willing to share public information.

Activity group 1: Building the capacity of journalists on investigative journalism / RTI / personal safety
The activities of this group include training of trainers with an international trainer, training of 250 journalists on RTI and safety, a handbook for journalists on RTI and a fellowship programme and competition for best investigative journalism using RTI Law
Output: Journalists have the capacity to use RTI in investigative journalism and to protect themselves while using it.
Result: Journalists are actively using RTI for the purposes of investigative journalism and simultaneously protect their personal safety.

Activity group 2: Raising public awareness on right to information and how to use the RTI Law
The activities of this group include public awareness campaigning, network of local "mediators" and a handbook and advocacy material for local communities on how to use the RTI Law for obtaining locally relevant information
Output: People have the knowledge of their constitutionally protected right to information and of the importance of the RTI Law to their lives as well as of how to submit requests for information.
Result: People actively utilize the RTI Law by making information requests to relevant public agencies.

Activity group 3: Improving the general climate for the successful implementation of the RTI Law
The activities of this group include local meetings with journalists and government information officers, high-level seminar on the implementation of the RTI act and establishing a loose network of civil society organizations and other potential stakeholders promoting RTI
Output: Power holders understand the possibilities and limitations of the RTI act and their role in its implementation
Result: Journalists, civil society activists and local mediators jointly work towards ensuring open and transparent society where public information is shared freely and without problems.

- Identification and usage of income generating opportunities


- On-farm and off-farm training, vocational training


- Awareness raising on gender based violence and reproductive health


- Training on disaster risk reduction, development of emergency plans and small scale mitigation measures

title: PRAGATI – “Promoting Resilient And sustainable urban Growth by Augmenting DRR capacity of Local Authorities Through active private sector Involvement”
description:
1. Brief introduction of project location containing geographical, economical, demographic, educational, health service, environment, and public infrastructure related information.

 

Kathmandu District

 

Kathmandu District is a district located in Kathmandu Valley, Province No. 3 of Nepal, a landlocked country in South Asia. It is one of the 75 districts of Nepal, covers an area of 395 km2 (153 sq mi), and is the most densely populated district of Nepal with 1,744,240 in 2011. The district's headquarters is Kathmandu Metropolitan City, also the capital of Nepal. Kathmandu district is one of the three districts located in Kathmandu Valley, which itself is located in the hills of Bagmati Zone, Central Development Region, Nepal. The district is located from 27°27′E to 27°49′E longitude and 85°10′N to 85°32′N latitude.

The people of the district are primarily Newars (Source: Census Report 2011 & District Profile, Kathmandu DDC).

 

As per the recommendation of DCC/DDRC, DCA has chosen the following two locations for project execution.

5.2.2 Need analysis containing problem tree related to proposed project and need identification process

 

The assessment for this action was undertaken during the period 15 December 2016 to 16 January 2017. More specifically, the field assessments were done on the following dates:

22 - 24 December 2016: Rapid Assessment through field visits to Shankharapur, Mahalaxmi, Karyabinayak and Mahamanjushree-Nagarkot (current Changunarayan) Municipalities and short qualitative interviews with private sector representatives

2 - 3 January 2017: Focal group and individual interviews at Shankharapur Municipality.

4 January 2017: Focal group and individual interviews in Nagarkot Municipality.

15 January 2017: Observation of Earthquake Safety day and interviews in Shankharapur Municipality mainly with private sector representatives (local cement blocks producers, rice mill owners, construction materials suppliers).

16 January 2017: Meetings and interviews with Nagarkot Naldum Tourism Management Committee, Homestay Association and with CBOs - Friends Help Groups.

The Needs assessment used mainly qualitative methods and information sources to identify the key issues and needs for the two selected municipalities. Analysing the collective experience of the consortium partners, DCA-ADRA-VSO served as the initial foundation of the formulation (ToRs) of the assessment. To avoid bias, the consortium employed an external consultant with extensive experience on Disaster Risk Management in Nepal and abroad to lead the Needs Assessment.  Initially a rapid assessment was conducted in four municipalities in Kathmandu Valley namely Mahamanjushree-Nagarkot, Mahalaxmisthan, Shankharapur and Karyabinayak Municipalities. The selection of these municipalities for the initial study was due to the presence of the consortium partners in these municipalities. The assessment included an initial disaster risk assessment and a need assessment for all the four municipalities. This involved physical observation and random interviews with local communities, private entities and the local authorities. Based on the findings from the four municipalities, two were selected for comprehensive disaster risk and needs assessment namely Mahamanjushree-Nagarkot Municipality (Current Changunarayan) from Bhaktapur District and Shankharapur Municipality in Kathmandu District.

 

Focal group discussions and individual interviews were then carried out with local authority and community representatives in each of the two municipalities including DDCs (current DCCs), District Administration Offices (DAO), Civil Society Organisations (CSOs), CBOs and NGOs working on disaster management and other development programmes. The assessment team also participated in the periodic District Disaster Relief Committee (DDRC) meetings. Consultation meetings (focus discussions) were carried out with selected private sector entities from both the municipalities. These included Nagarkot-Naldum Tourism Development Committee, National Home Stay Association in Nagarkot, and representatives from construction materials suppliers such as self-locking cement block manufacturers, timber suppliers, and food grain processing factories including rice mills, lentil mills, and a private hospital in Shankharapur.

 

Additionally, consultations were done with the representatives from Ministry of Urban Development (MoUD), National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC), and Municipal Association of Nepal (MUAN). Secondary data and information, such as case studies, research publications and policies were reviewed as a part of needs assessment. The material included the National Strategy for Resilient Urban Settlements, Nepal National Report -Third United Nations Conference on Housing and Sustainable Urban Development (Habitat III), study report conducted by Tribhuwan University on Earthquake Damage Assessment in the Traditional Town of Shankharapur and study report conducted by local partner NDRC on the impact of earthquake on elderly, People with Disability (PWDs) and how gender and ethnicity factor into the impact.

 

In the initial four municipalities assessed, a number of common problems were observed. These included (i) limited understanding of municipal authorities and local communities on disaster risk, (ii) limited understanding on exposure, hazards and vulnerability, including minimal information on emergency response and (iii) no platform for availing risk information. For example, authorities have documented neither information nor lessons from the 2015 earthquake response, and various level of impacts based on gender and age. Four areas of risk were identified in both the municipality: (1) Limited knowledge of information management system, as both municipalities lack hazard and exposure information, which could have been used for DRR related planning and execution. 2) Limited institutional governance to manage risk as both municipalities do not have LDRMPs nor abilities to incorporate associated risk information 3) Role of private sector is not recognized in development and execution of municipal plans. Despite substantial contribution to the 2015 earthquake response, the role of private sector has still not officially been recognised.  4) Limited capacity for Emergency Response, with Municipal authorities, community groups and private enterprises lacking proper emergency equipment (no stock keeping) and capacity to use this in an emergency response resulted into delayed response. Supply and maintenance of stock of SAR and life-saving materials is limited and lack of knowledge result in the limited use of material that are already available.

 

The proposed action aims to build the resilience of the Changunarayan and Shankharapur Municipalities through a holistic capacity enhancement approach, integrating local authorities, private sector and the most vulnerable local communities.

 

5.2.3 Linkage of project with national and sectoral policies of the Government of Nepal

DCA and IPs will coordinate with the municipality offices and other stakeholders working in the districts. The main purpose will be to coordinate with their ongoing and forthcoming development programs and project s with a view to avoiding duplication. The IPs will invite their representatives to participate in planning, implementation and review workshops at district level. They will also invite representative of concerned government district based development and administrative offices and authorities to visit the project community and to provide feedback for improving project implementation as necessary. Each IP at their district will coordinate with their respective district authority to build synergy in their ongoing programs and sustaining the lessons learnt of the project.

 

  1. Compliance the project activities with the national priority

This project has been designed with government policy, strategy and programs to provide support to the disaster vulnerable communities in the proposed districts. So, this project is in line with the national priority of government of Nepal to provide support and prepare them for future disaster.

 

  1. Proportional balance between hardware and software.

The action will provide disaster preparedness and rescue equipment, establish well equipped Disaster Risk Reduction Information Centre in the both municipalities, establish well equipped learning centers, emergency desk. Under these actions, the project will support physical infrastructure along with technical support. The action will also provide Mason training in both municipalities, Light Search and Rescue Equipment including rope, life jacket, shovels, helmets among others, first aid equipment for both Municipalities. The action will have Municipality Disaster Risk Management Plan (MDRMP), Disaster Risk Sensitive Tourism Development Plan, Risk sensitive contingency/emergency response plan of private hospital and small and medium scale enterprises, Municipality Emergency Preparedness and Response Plan, Household level DRM Plan at community homestay (MEPRP), Business contingency/emergency response plan of tourism industry (hotel/homestay) and District Disaster and Preparedness Plan in hand by the end of this project. In addition to this the action will also support to strengthen the knowledge of government authorities on information management and engage private sectors acknowledging their contribution for post disaster response. A total of 21,274 individuals (of 4579 households) from 5 wards in two municipalities will directly benefit from the action interventions, while 81,000 individuals (total population of two municipalities) will benefit indirectly.

 

5.3       Objectives and Activities with physical targets:

The main objective of the project is to increase preparedness and response capacities of local authorities and communities collaborating with the private sector contributing to the creation of resilient urban municipalities.

title: UN Joint  programme of support to LGCDP
description:
Empowering communities and community organisations to participate in local governance

  UNDP will draw on its more than ten years of experience of mobilising local communities to help citizens and communities engage more actively with local governments and for them to hold local governments to account. An important activity will be developing a mechanism for local bodies to systematically involve communities in planning and implementing programmes.



Enabling local body capacity building

  The Ministry of Local Development will be assisted to establish and implement a system for building up the capacity of local bodies to provide basic services inclusively and equitably. Two key support areas will be enabling DDCs to better backstop and mentor VDCs, and funding training programmes for local governments, community organisations, user groups and other service delivery agencies. These programmes will emphasise gender sensitivity and social inclusiveness and enable Nepal's 3,915 VDCs to make the best use of the grants of 1.5 million rupees plus ($20,000) they receive each year.



Enabling central government and national NGOs to support local governments

  UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA, and UNCDF will work together to strengthen the policy and national institutional framework for decentralisation, devolution and community development. This will include strengthening the capacity of the Ministry of Local Development to facilitate sector-wise devolution, to design and use a local government performance monitoring system and to mainstream gender equality and social inclusion issues into decentralisation processes. Other key tasks are to support the implementation of the national capacity building strategy for local bodies and to support the three local government associations (ADDCN, MuAN, NAVIN) to work on behalf of their member DDCs, VDCs and municipalities.

title: Managing Risk through Economic Development (MRED)
description:
1. To develop an effective and sustainable model of disaster risk reduction (DRR) in vulnerable communities of Nepal. This model will use hazard assessments, including climate modeling, to provide 3,000 households with a more sustainable DRR approach directly linked to their livelihoods, thereby mitigating the human and economic toll of natural disasters on their communities.
  2. Mobilization of gender/ ethnically-balanced DMCs through a concentrated process that focuses on those aspects of traditional DRR programming that have demonstrated potential for sustainability post-intervention.
  3. Training of DMCs in durable and sustainable techniques for mitigation, preparedness, response, and (if relevant) early warning.
  4. Participatory vulnerability and capacity assessments (VCAs) carried out by DMCs with communities and local government that provide an evidence-based platform for selection of DRR activities.
  5. Collaboration with climate expertise set up to a) assess long-term viability of proposed DRR activities, and b) determine if further risks need to be anticipated beyond those identified as priorities in the short-term.
  6. Plant and crop product and services assessments (for bioengineering, improved land/ watershed management and other complementary approaches).
  7. Local market assessments – tenure, high-demand/ high-value commodities cross-referenced with the plant/ crop species assessed for bioengineering, land/ watershed management and improved resiliency.
  8. Engage local and sub-national governments and private sector actors with community/DMC representatives in community selection, vulnerability and market assessments, and subsequent resource mobilization and decision-making.
  9. Facilitated planning of required risk mitigation measures and landscape-scale interventions.
  10. Assess land ownership/ usage patterns of marginal lands and determine target households accordingly.
  11. Train community groupsin protection and mitigation techniques and in the cultivation of disaster mitigating crops with strong income potential.
  12. Implement planned mitigation measures (based on plant/crop species identified under Outcome 1), including cultivation of crops that contribute to chronic disaster mitigation, through bioengineering or improved land/ water management (based on market and technical assessments).
  13. Train farmersin better seed varieties, improved planting techniques, new crops that are more resilient to local hazards.
  14. Link local input suppliers, extension actors and other training entities to ensure sustainability of the services.
  15. Establish maintenance plans for each mitigation measure, and where feasible, linked to economic opportunities from crops/products generated via these mitigation measures.
  16. Support micro and small enterprises, as necessary, for local value addition prior to sales, or for aggregation/ collective marketing and sales.
  17. Farmers, water and forest users and other localgroups formed, as necessary, to reinforce good technical practices and enhance market linkages/ economies of scale.
  18. Based on assessment findings and implementation experience, information regarding plant and crop species suitable for disaster mitigation and income generation compiled into at least two resource manuals in local languages and English for use by local government officials, other communities and partner agencies interested in replication.

title: Nepal Flood Response - Humanitarian Assistance
description: Funding under this investment represents Australia's support to Nepal in response to the recent devastating floods and landslides that have left over 1.7 million people in need of assistance. Flooding caused by heavy monsoon rains has resulted in over 150 deaths, damaged 65,000 homes and destroyed 64,000 hectares of standing crops across Nepal. Through this investment Australia will provide $2 million to the international relief effort, including $1 million through our humanitarian partnership with Australian non-government organisations and $1 million through the World Food Programme. The assistance will deliver emergency shelter, food, clean water and healthcare for those who have been affected by this disaster. Our contribution to the World Food Programme will enable it to treat 5,900 children under the age of five and 1,600 pregnant and nursing mothers for moderate acute malnutrition in the worst affected areas. In addition to this support, Australia is providing essential hygiene supplies and vital health services to 6,600 women and girls.

title: Building Agribusiness Capacity of Smallholder Farmers to Market Safe Produce of Good Quality
description:
Activity 1.1: Training of two government technical officers on agribusiness development in fresh produce chains;

Activity 1.2: Capitalizing on experiences and expertise from other countries in the region, develop training modules and guidelines for a Farm Business School to address farm to market agri-business linkages  and on horticultural chain management to address safety and quality across the supply chain.

Activity 1.3: Train 50 Officer level Master Trainers from the government agencies originating from central to district levels through a Farm Business School ToT (10-12 days) on farm-to-market agribusiness linkages and in horticultural chain management.

 

Activity 1.4:  With support from the master trainers, train local level trainers  (6 groups of 20 stakeholders, with a total of 120 participants), including government extension service providers (40) and Leader Farmers/Farmer Facilitators (80) on farm-to-market agribusiness linkages and horticultural chain management to assure the safety and quality of fresh produce.

Activity 2.1: Implement 60 Farm Business Schools (15 each district having 3 clusters, each cluster-5 groups) with training on horticultural chain management with the participation of existing production groups - preferably IPM groups - on the establishment of farm to market agribusiness linkages for produce outputs that are safe and of good quality;

Activity 2.2: Organize 6 observation visits of farmers’ group leaders to market sites and facilitate regular interactions with the traders, retailers and supermarkets to understand the market needs and opportunities for safe produce of good quality;

Activity 2.3: Support 60 farmers’ groups/cooperatives in the development of market linkages and in the establishment and operation of safe and quality crop production and marketing agribusinesses;

Activity 2.4: Provide specific trainings to the farmers’ groups in good post-harvest management practice - sorting, grading, cleaning, packaging, truthful labelling of safe and quality  produce, in line with market needs;  

Activity 2.5: Support famers’ groups in scaling up their agribusinesses activities through creating linkages with lending institutions, input supply sources, contract farming and other arrangements.

Activity 3.1:  Undertake a market survey and identify potential marketing channels and traders interested in handling and supplying safe produce of good quality;

Activity 3.2: Identify the requirements of traders and supermarkets for marketing safe and quality crop products;

Activity 3.3: Organize programmes that facilitate potential traders of safe and quality produce to interact with agri-businesses including supermarket chains;

Activity 3.4: Support traders to link them with production groups and agribusinesses and identification of marketing points or stalls;

Activity 3.5: Provide small equipment and materials to traders/retailers to assist them in differentiating their produce in the local market.

Activity 3.6: Assist traders in identifying and linking with local collectors for safe and quality produce.

Activity 3.7: Implement training and follow up support for produce collectors and traders (50) to trade produce that is differentiated on the basis of its safety and quality.

Activity 4.1: Document and disseminate success stories through printing media and video;

Activity 4.2: Implement a media campaign to promote the importance of assuring the safety of fresh produce for health and nutrition.

Activity 4.3: Develop and disseminate ICT materials on the benefits of safe produce of good quality;

title: ABA MERO PALO (Tipping Point)
description:
Activities under objective 1

  1. Project start up  ( Implementation strategy)
  2. Orient VCPC and DCPC on GBV (gender equality, GBV, child rights legal system with regard to child marriage, dowry, and VAW).
  3. Produce IEC materials (posters, audio visual, information package)   in child marriage in local language
  4. Allocate fund  to support innovative window opportunities  and  ideas, awareness  against child marriage and advance girls rights
  5. Support DCPC and VCPC awareness raising action (awareness campaigns, generating massage and information related to issue for wider sharing)
  6. Organize orientation to peer educators  on behavioral change communication, gender equality, GBV and community mobilization to eliminate child marriage and violence against women and girls
  7. Bio monthly review meetings/interaction with peer educators, VCPC and  change agent to review progress and issue and provide additional information and skill
  8. Support to felicitates influential "positive deviant"  (individual, families, community) who denounced harmful practices such child marriage, dowry and VAW
  9. Interaction among Aba Mero Palo UDAN, SAKCHAM and ATMANIRVAR projects of CARE Nepal  
  10. Campaign for domestic violence (child marriage) free VDC with collaboration with SAKCHAM team (only for Kapilbastu district)

Activities under objective 2

  1. Orient civil society organizations , groups to influence and mobilize  for the implementation of laws against child marriage and GBV
  2.  Organize orientation and impart skill and knowledge to the project team and partners on various issues that project is going to address (GBV, Do no Harm, child rights, legal instruments)
  3.  Develop information brief on GBV issues, based on religious scriptures and teachings
  4.  Conduct multi-religious seminars, specifically targeting men from different religions and including topics such as the effects and consequences of  early and unofficial marriage
  5.  Conduct Child marriage survey (six monthly)
  6.  Mobilization of Group Facilitator
  7.  Use mass media (community radio, street play  ) to reach large audiences coupled with interactive methodologies (call-in shows, discussion groups following serial dramas)
  8.  Produce facts sheets of  each  working  VDC,s social and economic costs of child marriage especially in the context of practices such as dowry and bride price
  9.  Trained and mobilize  60 selected  youth (18-20 years) as a  citizen  journalists  with media to communicate issue for policy action
  10. Interact with school management committees of all VDC and identify point persons in each school to raise awareness in schools
  11. Mobilize schools, teachers, district education office and school management committees to analyze reasons for drop-out of girls from schools and share widely the analysis for improvement
  12. Support to develop and implement mechanisms to better systematize marriage and birth registrations
  13. Promote public-private partnerships that are positioned to apply positive pressure to reduce early marriages, dowry and VAW
  14. Empower boys and girls  (10-14) by  developing their leadership and life skill / Mobilize boys  to organize issues based  (masculinity ) competitions for boys  in areas like drawing, cooking and stitching
  15. Capacity assessment/development of partners

Activities under objective 3

  1. Produce best practices and lesson learned to influence Government of Nepal’s to scale up of proven programming models policy, resource allocation  as well as  donors - to ensure they are tailored to support child marriage efforts globally.
  2. Support "Girls Not Brides" campaigns by organizing national campaigns on " Now It is my turn"   from districts to national level to employ  the programmatic lesson gained
  3. Develop mechanisms for community monitoring/audits of child marriage through VDC, Child clubs, VCPC and share analysis twice a year  for policy advocacy
  4. Organize every year  public hearing in each working district to share  existing laws and policy implementation against child marriage and dowry
  5. Engage with national coalitions to monitor the implementation of public policies and support advocacy initiatives at national levels
  6. Advocacy in country trainings
  7. Formation and strengthening Local Advisory Council
  8. Documentation in six monthly basis (Audio, Video, Info graphics, Briefs, fact sheet)

 

 

Activities under objective 4

 

  1. Orient  Civil Society / VDC secretaries on child marriage and GBV and its social and economic cost and role of VDC  to empower eliminate GBV and child
  2. Facilitate each VDC to develop strategy/action plan   to eliminate child marriage and dowry  and girls education program
  3. Lobby with major political parties to denounce against child marriage, VAW and dowry and enforce code conduct for members
  4. Conduct parental education monthly session in each ward
  5. Formation of child (girls up to 20 yrs) clubs in each ward
  6. Establish culture of celebrating "fatherhood" by organizing local campaigns targeting specific groups of men and boys, such as married men (focusing on maternal, newborn and child health) men as fathers.
  7. Support to existing boys clubs for raising voice against child marriage and dowry
  8. Conduct intergenerational dialogues  at VDC level (SRH, GBV etc)
  9. Interaction  with VCPC , school management committee , religious leaders, media people  in challenging attitudes of gender inequity, to address child marriage and GBV
  10. Engage parents, caregivers and school dropout girls to delay marriage and continue education (skill development, income generating activities)
  11. Engage/train  boys ages 15-18 in gender trainings  for gender equitable attitudes, behaviors and  to avoid and prevent early marriage, dowry and VAW
  12. Community outreach mobilization and mass media (  evidence of sustained change in attitudes and behavioral intentions)  for prevention of child marriage and GBV
  13. Mobilize boys clubs to organize issues based  (masculinity ) competitions for boys  in areas like drawing, cooking and stitching,
  14. Collaborate with VDC and  Schools to establish  scholarship scheme for PVSE girls
  15. Publish stories, interviews of boys and their parents who declare for not engaging in child marriage and dowry.
  16. SIYB training and seed money support  to adolescent girls for business start

title: Enhancing Sustainability and Profitability of the Carpet and Pashmina Industries in the Kathmandu Valley (Switch-Asia)
description:
Activity Cluster 1: Promoting and facilitating the switch to sustainable production.

  • Develop cleaner production awareness campaigns through workshops and its wider dissemination through Central Carpet Industries Association (CCIA), Nepal Wool Dyeing Industry Association (NWDIA) and the National Pashmina Industries Association (NPIA) by distribution of information packs.
  • Undertake assessment of sample production units and develop CP implementation plans.
  • Lead training workshops for the design, implementation and maintenance of CP techniques for unit owners, managers and workers.
  • Develop model units for dyeing and washing sub-sectors and carry out cross-visits.
  • Produce and disseminate cleaner production practice operating manual for carpet dyeing, washing and pashmina operations.
  • Provide technical support to implement cleaner production activities to the participating industries.

title: Building Resilience to Landslides through Support for Community-Based Rehabilitation and Mitigation Actions and the Establishment of Early Warning Systems in Nepal
description:
Activity 1.1.1: Working with ICIMOD and government partners at both national and district-levels, review existing survey results and High Resolution Satellite Imagery (Digital Global, NASA,.SERVIR) of identified district to determine areas and communities where threat and interventions are most critical,

Activity 1.1.2: Development of user-friendly Hazard Mapping and Vulnerability Analysis (HVMA) Tool Kit which incorporates concepts of the Geo-Design Approach prioritization of communities  where preparedness and mitigation activities are most required – with particular focus on local agriculture context,

Activity 1.1.3: In prioritized communities, conduct on-the-ground AHVMA to identify critical landslides-affected and prone areas, which impact on  agricultural production and irrigation infrastructure – using simple, yet scientifically informed tools,

Activity 1.1.4: Review and/or establish comprehensive watershed management plans through a community-based integrated livelihoods.

 Activity 1.2.1: Working with the Department of Soil Conservation and Watershed Management, implement a campaign to seal off smaller land cracks in order to avoid water infiltration and expansion.

Activity 1.2.2: Stabilize the prioritized landslides with a combination of bioengineering techniques (plantations, bamboo, ground cover, etc.) and engineering structures (gabion walls, check dams, etc.)

Activity 1.2.3: Provide training in contingency planning to community members within existing cooperatives, Watershed Management Committees or Forest User Groups.

Activity 1.2.4: Work with MOAD, provide training to farmer organizations and cooperatives on improved technologies for agro-forestry, slope stabilization and soil conservation.

 Activity 2.1.1: Provide key leaders from MOAD and MOFSC at both national and district levels (DADO, DSCO) with tools, protocols and training for identifying landslide affected prone agricultural areas;

 

Activity 2.1.2: Working with partners of the Landslide Sub-Groups for Mitigation and Capacity Building, test and refine community-based mitigation and rehabilitation strategies and technologies in coordination with existing government partners to promote scale-up and replication to further districts;

Activity 2.1.3: Lessons learnt and best practice documents are created and shared through stakeholder dissemination events and used to advocate for continued budget support for the maintenance and operation of established systems;

Activity 2.1.4: Conduct work shop for the incorporation of best practices and strategies into development programming at the relevant ministries;

title: Reaching Down and scaling Up: Strengthening resilience of local communities to disasters.
description:
1.1.1  Design and disseminate Behavior Change Communication (BCC) materials on DRM/disaster resilient community based on hazard profile in the project locations

1.1.2  Organize awareness raising campaigns in the communities and schools on DRM

1.1.3  Conduct inclusive Vulnerability and Capacity Assessments (VCA) of the communities and disseminate the information through hazard maps

 

1.2.1 Identify the most vulnerable households and individuals such as elderlies, persons with disabilities, women headed households and the poorest

1.2.2 Assist most vulnerable households and individuals selected to develop their household DRM plan

1.2.3 Provide personalized support for the selected most vulnerable households and individuals to implement their household/individual DRM plan

2.1.1  Form and train village and community level inclusive Local Disaster Management Committees on government's LDRMP Guideline and process

2.1.2 Form and train inclusive task forces on their roles and responsibilities for risk reduction

2.1.3 Develop inclusive Local Disaster Risk Management Plans for village and communities using findings from VCAs

2.2.1 Engage DMCs and task force members on simulation and drilling of Local Disaster Risk Management Plans

2.2.2 Identify and promote the use of traditional, indigenous and local knowledge and practices on DRM including on early warning systems to build the culture of safety in the communities

2.2.3 Demonstrate low cost and replicable small scale mitigation measures (drainages, irrigation canals, bi-engineered spurs, culverts), model joint projects with VDCs/district authorities

3.1.1 Provide trainings on first aid, light search and rescue, early warning, damage need assessments, water and sanitation to task force and DMC members

3.1.2 Train Masons and disseminate information of the government/National Reconstruction Authority on building back better, safer and accessible among the communities rebuilding their houses

3.1.3 Provide emergency equipment and emergency fund for Disaster Management Committees and task forces

3.2.1 Mainstream and integrate DRM into education sector through selected inclusive school-based DRM interventions including temporary and safe learning centers

3.2.2 Promote recovery of accessible water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructures that contribute towards risk reduction

3.2.3 Advocate for inclusive preparedness and recovery policies and plans through networking, collaboration and capacity building measures on policies and Core Humanitarian Standards

4.1.1 Prepare detailed operational plan for Cash Based Interventions- CBIs (Cash for Work and Unconditional Cash Transfer)

4.1.2 Implement CBIs to rehabilitate community assets

4.1.3 Conduct the survey impact of CBIs in local market and in reducing negative coping strategies of vulnerable people

4.2.1 Train and provide inputs to support off-seasonable vegetable production

4.2.2 Train and provide inputs for livestock raising

4.2.3 Assist vulnerable people on off-farm enterprises including blacksmiths to recover their small scale business/enterprises

title: Public Financial Management Support Multi-Donor Trust Fund Contribution (Nepal) - Phase 2
description:
The objective of the MDTF is to strengthen the performance, transparency and accountability in public financial management in Nepal.

The Key Results expected from the projects to be funded through the MDTF are:

1. Improved resource management as a result of strengthened PFM systems and processes,

2. Increased awareness and oversight of government PFM processes by diverse constituencies ,

3. Better knowledge of value for money challenges and PFM governance gaps, contributing to improved design of PFM interventions at the country and sector level.

The trust fund PDO will be attained through implementation of various sub-projects designed and implemented with support from the MDTF. The MDTF will be used as a vehicle to support a wide range of activities based on priorities set by the government and development partners broadly categorized under three broad dimensions: Supply, Demand and Knowledge.

The MDTF will support activities that will: (a) strengthen the PFM systems and processes (the supply side); (b) strengthen institutions of accountability and civil society to enhance their oversight of PFM processes and performance (the demand side); and (c) deepen knowledge about current PFM practices and options for improvement.

Purpose 1: Livelihoods strengthened and diversified

SP1.1: Household Income is Increased.

SP 1.2 Household Capacity to cope with shocks is increased.

SP 1.3 Integration of vulnerable households into value chain is strengthened.

SP 1.4 Women’s control over productive resource is increased.

 

Purpose 2: Health and nutritional status of pregnant and lactating women, children under five and their families is improved.

SP 2.1 Household health, WASH and nutrition behaviors are improved.

SP 2.3 Use of quality health services by women and children is increased.

SP 2.4 National, regional and district mechanisms for combating malnutrition are effective.

 

Purpose 3: Ability of households and communities to mitigate, adapt to, and recover from shocks and stresses is strengthened.

SP 3.1 Communities and local authorities implement integrated DRM and CCA plans

SP 3.2 Vulnerable households utilize information on natural hazards and climate change in their decision making.

SP 3.3 Local disaster early warning systems are effective.

SP 3.4 National, regional and district mechanisms for climate change adaptation and disaster risk reduction planning are established.

3.6 Actively observe/intervene CBPOs’ regular maintenance on those infrastructures.

3.7 Livelihood support.

4.2 Workshop on LDRMP revision - Technical supports for creation of better LDRMP.

4.3 Support for coordination and linkage with stakeholders (CBPOs' Association, CDMC, Nepal Red Cross Society, Nepal Police, Army, DDRC, DDC etc.)

5. Implemented DRR activities at school level. (Output no. 3)

5.1 Collection of successful cases

5.2 Identify targeted middle schools.

5.3 Introduce DRR activities including evacuation drill at middle schools.

6.1 Organize sharing visit with other agencies implementing DRR project against river flood.

6.2 Organize coordination meeting of stakeholders working for development of Madi.

6.3 Participate in Flagship 4 or any other agency's conference about DRR.

7.2 Sharing Meeting at VDC Level (technical supports to assess explicit & implicit risks and to learn possible measures against those risks by expert).

7.4.1 Refreshment on Discussion meeting with beneficiaries

7.4.3 Construction of Learning Center (size: 14x14/ 3 rooms)

8.2 Support to produce hazard maps through participatory discussions and to understand high risk points in their community

title: Creating Enabling Environments for Nutrition-Sensitive Food and Agriculture to Address Malnutrition
description:
1.1 Map existing policies, regulations and institutions that cover crop-related NUS from a food system perspective.

1.2 Review policies, regulations and institutions affecting crop-related NUS, identifying critical policy issues and technical gaps that may exist in relation to supporting production and dietary diversity.

1.3 Develop specific recommendations to address the policy and programmatic gaps which will foster the diversification of crops and diets that tap the potential of NUS (based on activities listed under item 2 below).

1.4 Organize national multi-stakeholders policy dialogues on challenges and options promoting pathways out of malnutrition, with a focus on crop-related NUS, and assist Governments in adopting new/revised policy frameworks.

2.1 Conduct targeted analysis on malnutrition, crop diversity and dietary/food consumption analyses in the selected geographic areas and populations according to the incidence and prevalence of malnutrition, identifying key features and main challenges.

2.2 Identify 1-2 selected underutilized crop(s) with a known high nutritional value that are part of traditional diets, and with potential for expanding their role along food value chain.

2.3 Conduct factor/policy analysis along supply/value chain to promote market development and commercialization, through field survey and interviewing relevant stakeholders including farmers, processors, traders, and urban/rural consumers for the selected crop-related NUS to identify policy, regulatory and institutional constraints and potential for production, consumption and market development. The study will also cover some cross-cutting issues: such as gender equality and decent rural employment.

2.4 Conduct technical analysis on the productivity gaps and potential for selected underutilized crop(s) from field to market and requirements for policy intervention and knowledge transfer.

3.1 Provide a synthesis report based on lessons learnt from the country studies.

3.2 Capacity building and knowledge sharing of national studies at regional level.

title: Okhaldhunga Recovery and Resilience Program
description:
• Initiate outreach to communities immediately to address high rates of non-compliance and provide basic information about construction standards that will need to be met.
  • Similarly, initial outreach to communities will look to address reasons related with HHs not starting reconstruction in close collaboration with CRCs.
  • Identify and contract technical resource organization(s), institutes or technical persons to deliver technical support in project activities like both the skilled and unskilled mason trainings, construction of low cost model houses, IEC material development etc and involve local contractors (who oversee and direct gangs of laborers and masons in the construction of homes).
  • Provide top-up support and targeted technical assistance to extremely vulnerable households who need in kick-starting the construction or rehabilitation of their homes. This may be applied as financial support (cash transfer) and/or material transport or at one of the five construction stages including, for example, demolishing their damaged homes and removing rubble.
  • Build low cost model houses (one per ward and 65 in total) through vocation and on-the-job mason training. The low-cost model houses will be built for the most vulnerable household in the ward. CRS will adopt the vulnerability criteria developed by NRA for the selection of model house beneficiary. Series of consultation meetings will be held with communities, ward citizen forums and Gaon Palika leadership to ensure that most eligible model house beneficiary is selected through a very transparent process. Upon completion of the model house, the property will be handed over to the beneficiary.
  • CRS will use Central Level Project Implementation Unit (CLPIU) approved model house designs including Stone Masonry Mud Mortar (SMM), SMM with attic roof and RCC for CRS Gorkha Program approved on 09 August 2017. CRS will positively adopt any other models that have been approved by NRA or CLPIU by the time implementation is started.
  • CRS will engage a technical agency to ensure that the low-cost model houses are constructed in a short span of time considering the housing needs of the most vulnerable households. Strong technical oversight from the technical agency through experienced human resources will help in high quality structures. The construction firm will also be engaged in conducting trainings for masons. CRS implementing partners and the construction firm will work in close coordination to ensure that the social mobilization aspects of model house construction and mason training is adequately integrated.
  • CRS will adopt “mobile masons” approach to ensure that house owners and workers involved in construction get adequate on-site technical support through direct supervision. Such support will ensure that the houses built are in compliant with NRA norms. Through this mechanism CRS will engage skilled and unskilled masons to support families and labor working at the household level.  Each mason will be expected to visit every household at each of the 5 key stages of construction:  layout, foundation, wall, roof and fixations (doors and windows) to verify that the house meets guidelines for earthquake resistance.
  • Work closely with its key implementing partners on all community mobilization activities, including outreach to individual families with key information about the GoN processes and EQ-safety measures; animation and capacity development of pre-existing community management structures (whether the CRC or other); identification of extremely vulnerable households in need of specialized assistance; as well as monitoring of all key project activities. To facilitate this process in the field, CRS will depute 11 social mobilization officers through the project.
  • Coordinate with key stakeholders at the district and VDC levels with a concern for working closely with NRA engineers who oversee, review and approve household construction.
  • While starting the project, CRS will conduct a quick assessment to understand the most updated needs and trends in the communities around capacity building of households in general and masons in specific regarding reconstruction of their houses. If majority of the masons has already received training and supply for the skilled labor has increased through Unskilled Labor Training (Vocational training masonry) by other NGOs, CRS will focus on the information, promotion and capacity building for retrofitting techniques. This may require changing some of the key activities and indicators in the Objective 1 for which detailed amendment with scale and scope of the activity targets will be shared with NRA accordingly. The refresher trainings will also include correction manual/retrofitting which will help masons adhere to EQ resistant construction techniques in case of already constructed houses.
  • On-the-job training on retrofitting will include demonstration of such techniques in existing houses. CRS will conduct detailed technical assessments for identifying appropriate retrofitting techniques for different conditions in coordination with local NRA engineers.
  • For the skilled and unskilled mason trainings CRS will prioritize identification of participants from local communities. However, recognizing the fact that significant number of masons/construction workers from terai and other regions of the country are engaged in reconstruction work, CRS will facilitate their participation in mason trainings wherever possible. Series of orientation meetings will be held at the community level for selection of training beneficiaries. In order to encourage participation of needy and motivated women members, CRS will hold orientation meetings with existing women savings/mothers’ groups to ensure that accurate information about the mason trainings is available to women members for them to take an informed decision about participating in trainings.

title: Integrating Water and Sanitation Services to Urban Poor Communities in two Municipalities of Nepal
description:
The project aims to support the following number of people of the poor urban settlements based on the poverty mapping report and field assessment of Kamalamai and Itahari Municipalities:

  • A total of 5 settlements in wards 11 and 12 with population of 3193 (623 households(HHs)) where more than 65% people are below the poverty line;
  • A total of 17 settlements of urban poor and squatter communities in four different wards with population of 911HHs.

 The major activities are-

  • Based on the preparation and assessment of water, environmental sanitation and hygiene improvement plan, provide safe water, affordable adequate sanitation and hygiene education to the targeted people of Kamalamai and Itahari Municipalities;
  • Reduce the burden of collecting water, ensure equity of distribution, increase optimization of water use and reduce water borne diseases as well as increase dignity;
  • Increase the capacity of civil society groups and 2 municipalities to work together to effectively implement water and sanitation improvement plans and promote environmental sanitation;
  • Based on the lessons learnt, contribute in effective engagement and influencing municipal and central level urban water and sanitation programming and monitoring activities.

title: Improving Functionality of Water Supply Services in Nepal
description:
Advisory and capacity development services to government, non-government actors at national and sub-national level for: 

  • Improving enabling environment for functionality of water supply services
  • Improving performance of WSS actors for effective service delivery
  • Improving governance, gender equity, social inclusion, knowledge management and synergy (cross cutting)
  • EXTENDED (2015)
  • Update of existing functionality strategy based on updated functionality status as  per functionality mapping concept  (FRWS Workshop, Nov 2014) and get it endorsed from DWASHCC
  • A plan of action showing all partially functional and non-functional schemes getting converted into well functional within specified time period (2015 - 2017) and get it endorsed from DWASHCC
  • Organize half-day workshop in the district by inviting DWASHCC members and other stakeholders
  • Organize a field visit for Joint Monitoring Team to observe improvement of schemes (41 schemes)
  • Organize a district level public hearing on FRWS in order to reflect the voice of the public in the planning cycle of district Nov 2015
  • Compile questionnaire for collecting functionality status & scheme ranking  database (116 schemes in 21 VDCs of 4 programme districts)
  • 2-days orientation training program on GPS to WS technicians/LRPs
  • GPS data collection of  intake, reservoir tank, public/community tap, served/unserved settlements of 106 schemes
  • PCS/Maintenance & Repair Unit is made visible in the premises of WSSDO with separate room, name plate of unit-in-charge, furnished with required furniture, shelves, desktop computer, laser printer, etc.
  • A board with citizen charter displaying various post construction support services to be provided to schemes
  • Information about all schemes is compiled & installed at the desktop of PCS Unit
  • TOT for PCS/ Maintenance & Repair Unit on (i) Technical aspect -Repair & maintenance (ii) Management aspect - Scheme management & Financial management of schemes (accounting system/ tariff set up, O&M fund management, (iii) WSP etc.
  • Orientation training to PCS/Maintenance & Repair Unit to develop process of planning based on feedback from self-assessment forms, functionality mapping and ranking
  • Support to PCS/Maintenance & Repair Unit to organize a VMW training by inviting VMWs various schemes
  • Orientation training to 3 representatives (Chairman, Secretary, VMW/Active member) from 106 schemes on self-assessment process & services of PCS Unit
  • Support for  assessing markets, quality of materials available in the market and monitoring the services of VMWs.
  • Support to private sector development
  • Design PSA messages (5-7) for the general public regarding the quality of material and quality of construction prior to scheme construction
  • Design hoarding boards (at least 2 numbers) in appropriate size and display all 5-7 PSA messages in the board in local language understandable to general public
  • A simplified version of self-assessment guideline for scheme operation prepared
  • Local Resource Persons (LRPs) looking after 5 VDCs (3 LRPs responsible for 9 schemes of 5 VDCs) are trained on Self-assessment guideline and other TOT along with 3-4 staffs of PCS/Maintenance & Repair Unit
  • Each LRP together with government officials (wherever possible) carry out self-assessment exercise in the selected schemes within the VDC of his/her responsibility and teach WUSC members & VMW how to carry out self-assessment of schemes and other aspects of scheme management to make them fully functional.
  • Organize an observation visit to FEDWASUN members & some staffs of PCS/Maintenance & Repair Unit together to visit fully functioning schemes within district and have interaction with WUSC members.
  • Organise 3 days TOT on Social Accountability (Community Score Card, Public Hearing & Social Auditing) training (one day practical in one of the schemes identified by district FEDWASUN) for 4 members of FEDWASUN (Resource Person is provided by SNV Nepal)
  • Apply SA tool to another scheme of the district by trained members of FEDWASUN

title: Distribution of Mountain Search and Rescue Equipment to Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Nepal
description:
The Embassy of the Republic of Korea donated 17 different types of search and rescue gears and equipment to the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Government of Nepal. 

1. Ground Penetraing Radar(GPR) - 1 no.

- Capacity of detecting more than 20 meters of snow and ice below ground (not available with us) - Capable of being detached from the main frame and of being carried and used by human arms/hands in case that cart is not available (uneven ground, hilly area, slippery snow/ice etc.)

 

2. Metal Detector - 5 nos.

- Capacity of detecting more than 20/15/10 meters of snow and ice below ground - Should be hand carried / RECCO metal detector

 

3. Avalanche Detector - 5 nos. 

- RECCO-level high quality detector with detecting capacity more than 20/15/10 meters of snow and ice below ground / Similar product/device available from Black Diamond (BT Guide Beacon)

 

4. Avalanche Probe - 20 nos. 

-Mix of 3 meters and 5 meters/ Only upto 320cm available. Black Diamond Quickdraw Tour Prove 320cm

 

5. Avalanche Beacon - 5 nos. 

- Black Diamond Guide BT Beacon

 

6. Outdoor Helmet - 20 nos. 

- Black diamond Half dome helmet

 

7. Ice Axe - 10 nos.

- Black Diamond Raven Ice axe with grip

 

8. Pick Axe - 10 nos.

- To break hard snow and ice / Black Diamond Venom Hammer

 

9. Mountaineering Harness - 10 nos.

- Black Diamond Couloir Harness

 

10. Crampons - 20 nos.

-Black Diamond Sabretooth Pro/Clip

 

11. Stretchers - 5 nos.

 

12. Climbing Ropes - 10 nos.

- 8.5mm, 60m Dry Black Diamond

 

13. Carabiners - 20 nos. 

- Black Diamond Rocklock Screwgate

 

14. Quick Draws - 20 nos. 

- Black Diamond Positron Quickdraw 12/16cm

 

15. Gamow Bag (PAC) - 1 no.

- Price for new one, but used ones are available for cheaper prices

 

16. Rescue Bags - 5 nos.

-Exped search and rescue bag 50L

 

17. Hypothermia Management Kit - 10 nos.

 

18. Mountaineering Shovels - 20 nos.

- Black Diamond Lynx shovel

title: 467GLO1007.26 (ED) - CAP EFA: Capacity Assessment for Non-formal Education in Nepal
description: According to GMR 2011, Nepal has illiterate population of 7.6 million (or 42% of the total) of whom 67 percent are women. Literacy rates vary by ecological regions with the Hills with highest literacy rate (55%) and the Mountains with the lowest (41%). However, the Terai has the highest number of illiterates followed by the Hills. Large disparities exist between male and female literacy rates in all age groups. According to the 2001 census, the literacy rate for six years and older males (66%) is 23 percentage points higher than that for the same age group of females (43%). The youth literacy rate (15 to 24 years) of 70 percent is significantly higher than the adult literacy rate (age 15 years and above) of 48 percent The weak capacity in the Nepal education sector in general, and in literacy and NFE in particular, have been highlighted in recent studies, discussions, consultations, workshops and reports on education in Nepal. There is general consensus that the capacity of the Ministry of education in general and NFEC in particular is very weak to plan, develop, implement and manage programs aimed at increasing literacy and lifelong education. There is lack of capacity for evidence-based planning and lack of adequate capacity for managing the NFE sub-sector. Nepal is one of the 20 CapEFA countries in the biennium 2009 - 2011 and is being engaged in the capacity development of Non-formal Education staff and CLC management committee members mainly focusing Education Sector Analysis for NFE sub-sector, identification of potential target group and beneficiaries, setting benchmark and target indicator values, and action planning for operationalization of reviewed NFE policy for achieving target indicator values. The outcomes of this effort resulted in the enhancement of capacity of leadership, ownership and harmonization; institutional capacity; organizational capacity; quality and equity; and knowledge-generation for capacity development in the NFE sub-sector as envisaged in Cap EFA Strategic Framework. The concrete and tangible outputs that have evolved so far include: (a) National Plan of Action for developing and expanding CLCs, (b) Establishment of NFE-MIS in three pilot districts, (c) Reliable estimates of current literacy skills through literacy survey. In this context, following a request from the Non formal Education Centre for UNESCO's support in the NFE sub-sector, it has been agreed that UNESCO will arrange for the continuation of support for capacity development in the implementation of the NFE Sub-sector Programme. As such identification of what key capacities are already developed/existing and what additional capacities are needed in the NFE sub-sector in order to enable the country to be on track with EFA goals by 2015 is crucial. Hence UNESCO Kathmandu aspires to further play an active role in assisting the MoE in the area of Literacy and non-formal education. In collaboration with MOE, UNESCO Bangkok, UNESCO HQ, UIL and other relevant partners, the Office will provide support to the MOE for the development of capacity development plan for literacy and NFE subsector in Nepal.

title: Digo Samudaya Eastern DRR Phase III
description:
Tripartite Agreement sign off – Local Governments, Habitat local Partner and Habitat Nepal, will sign an agreement on funding contributions, roles and responsibilities throughout the duration of the project. 

• Project Kick-Off Meeting - an orientation about the project with the staff of the partner organisations and local governments to share project objectives with local communities. 

• Selection of communities - 10 different local communities, 5 in Jhapa and 5 in Saptari, will be selected, in consultation with local government and local partners. 

• LDMC engagement – The Ward-Level LDMC will be a governmental partner in planning and delivering community-based DR3 interventions along with the NGO partner. 

• Low-cost, disaster-resilient housing designs – A New Zealand university will be a partner to assist in the technical analysis of low-cost disaster-resilient housing designs developed by Habitat and Municipal engineers. The designs will be incorporated into local government building requirements or codes, and Habitat will support the local government system in monitoring and enforcing these minimum requirements by offering training to governmental staff.

 • PASSA group formation - PASSA groups with a good representation from the communities, including women and PWD,s will be formed within communities. Habitat Nepal with our partners will facilitate the PASSA members through the eight sessions in the program. PASSA groups will also identify the most vulnerable families within their community, to be eligible for top-up grants. 

• PASSA training sessions - As an outcome of these sessions, PASSA groups identify the disaster risks facing the communities and suggest the course of actions necessary to mitigate those risks. Similarly, they will discuss various issues related to most vulnerable families, issues of women, PWDs, old age people, children and others. 

• LDMC/PASSA collaboration – Government and Community groups on DRR join in preparing DR3 projects within the community and how this will be resourced and implemented. LDMC will raise funds and provide technical assistance to the community. 

• Mason Training- Mason’s are vital to delivering safe shelter in communities in terms of awareness and practice. Masons will be trained on the importance of safe shelter techniques and practice. 

• Lands Title Office engagement - The local office will be key to owning the joint-titling registration process. Training and process development will be provided through a Civil Rights expert or Lawyer. Having the backing and approval from the Major/Deputy Mayor will ensure greater adoption and acceptance of this new practice. 

• Women’s Savings Groups to build community awareness of Joint-Titles – The DFAT BPP Micro-Finance project in the same communities uses women’s savings groups to offer and disperse loans to low-income families. These groups of women will receive orientation sessions on Women’s Inheritance Rights and information on fee discounts/exemptions for the new registration process.

 • Youth Groups to promote Safe Housing and Inheritance Rights – Through local Youth groups and the Habitat Young Leaders Build (HYLB) program, youth will be mobilised to organise community awareness raising events to promote Safe Housing standards and Women’s Inheritance Rights issues. Youth groups will raise resources to conduct these events

title: NPL Pooled Appeal Earthquake 2015 SoF: 99700163
description:
NPL Pooled Appeal Earthquake 2015 SoF: 99700163 

On Saturday, 25th of April 2015, a powerful earthquake of magnitude 7.8 on the Richter scale hit Nepal. The epicentre of the earthquake was in Gorkha District, about 80 km north-west of the capital, Kathmandu. The quake was felt as far as Dhaka in Bangladesh and Delhi in India, making it the biggest earthquake Nepal has seen in 80 years. Less than 3 weeks later, another earthquake measuring 7.3 in magnitude struck on Tuesday May 12th with an epicentre southeast of Kodari, in Sindhupalchowk District, 76 km northeast of Kathmandu. The heavy destruction and damage resulting from the first earthquake was further exacerbated as some eight million people across 39 of Nepal’s 75 districts were affected, with 14 districts considered to be the ‘worst affected’.

A total of 498,852 houses were categorized as fully collapsed or damaged beyond repair and 256,697 houses were partly damaged, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. In addition, numerous schools were destroyed and damaged and the earthquakes greatly impacted on public health infrastructures.  As of 30th October 2015, UN OCHA reported that 8,891 individuals lost their lives and 22,309 people were injured.  From that figure, 2,737 children lost their lives and 2,107 children were injured.

Save the Children adapted and updated its response projects to ensure they are relevant. One of the major initiatives over the last several months was to focus on beneficiary selection (versus blanket coverage), so that the most affected and marginalized people receive benefits
